 Over half of the survey respondents preferred the term "soda", which was dominant in the Northeastern United States, California, and the areas surrounding Milwaukee and St. The term "pop", which was preferred by 25% of the respondents, was most popular in the Midwest and Pacific Northwest, while the genericized trademark "coke", used by 12% of the respondents, was most popular in the Southern United States. The term "tonic" is distinctive to eastern Massachusetts, although usage is declining.In the English-speaking parts of Canada, the term "pop" is prevalent, but "soft drink" is the most common English term used in Montreal.In the United Kingdom and Ireland, the term "fizzy drink" is common. U.S. soft drinks 7-Up or Sprite are called "lemonade" in the UK.In other languages, various names are used: descriptive names as "non-alcoholic beverages", equivalents of "soda water", or generalized prototypical names. In the medieval Middle East, a variety of fruit-flavored soft drinks were widely drunk, such as sharbat, and were often sweetened with ingredients such as sugar, syrup and honey. it was a sweetened drink with lemon flavor and containing cream of tartar. 'Manays Cryste' was a sweetened cordial flavored with rosewater, violets or cinnamon.Another early type of soft drink was lemonade, made of water and lemon juice sweetened with honey, but without carbonated water. The Compagnie des Limonadiers of Paris was granted a monopoly for the sale of lemonade soft drinks in 1676. Vendors carried tanks of lemonade on their backs and dispensed cups of the soft drink to Parisians. In the late 18th century, scientists made important progress in replicating naturally carbonated mineral waters. In 1767, Englishman Joseph Priestley first discovered a method of infusing water with carbon dioxide to make carbonated water when he suspended a bowl of distilled water above a beer vat at a local brewery in Leeds, England. His invention of carbonated water (later known as soda water, for the use of soda powders in its commercial manufacture) is the major and defining component of most soft drinks.Priestley found that water treated in this manner had a pleasant taste, and he offered it to his friends as a refreshing drink. In 1772, Priestley published a paper entitled Impregnating Water with Fixed Air in which he describes dripping oil of vitriol (or sulfuric acid as it is now called) onto chalk to produce carbon dioxide gas and encouraging the gas to dissolve into an agitated bowl of water. Swedish chemist Torbern Bergman invented a generating apparatus that made carbonated water from chalk by the use of sulfuric acid. Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius started to add flavors (spices, juices, and wine) to carbonated water in the late eighteenth century. Thomas Henry, an apothecary from Manchester, was the first to sell artificial mineral water to the general public for medicinal purposes, beginning in the 1770s. His recipe for 'Bewley's Mephitic Julep' consisted of 3 drachms of fossil alkali to a quart of water, and the manufacture had to 'throw in streams of fixed air until all the alkaline taste is destroyed'.Johann Jacob Schweppe developed a process to manufacture bottled carbonated mineral water. He founded the Schweppes Company in Geneva in 1783 to sell carbonated water, and relocated his business to London in 1792. In 1843, the Schweppes company commercialized Malvern Water at the Holywell Spring in the Malvern Hills, and received a royal warrant from King William IV.It was not long before flavoring was combined with carbonated water. A variant of soda in the United States called "phosphate soda" appeared in the late 1870s. It became one of the most popular soda fountain drinks from 1900 through the 1930s, with the lemon or orange phosphate being the most basic. The drink consists of 1 US fl oz (30 ml) fruit syrup, 1/2 teaspoon of phosphoric acid, and enough carbonated water and ice to fill a glass. Soft drinks soon outgrew their origins in the medical world and became a widely consumed product, available cheaply for the masses. By the 1840s, there were more than fifty soft drink manufacturers in London, an increase from just ten in the 1820s. Carbonated lemonade was widely available in British refreshment stalls in 1833, and in 1845, R. White's Lemonade went on sale in the UK. For the Great Exhibition of 1851 held at Hyde Park in London, Schweppes was designated the official drink supplier and sold over a million bottles of lemonade, ginger beer, Seltzer water and soda-water. There was a Schweppes soda water fountain, situated directly at the entrance to the exhibition.Mixer drinks became popular in the second half of the century. As the quinine powder was so bitter people began mixing the powder with soda and sugar, and a basic tonic water was created. A persistent problem in the soft drinks industry was the lack of an effective sealing of the bottles. Carbonated drink bottles are under great pressure from the gas, so inventors tried to find the best way to prevent the carbon dioxide or bubbles from escaping. Hiram Codd devised a patented bottling machine while working at a small mineral water works in the Caledonian Road, Islington, in London in 1870. His Codd-neck bottle was designed to enclose a marble and a rubber washer in the neck. The bottle was pinched into a special shape to provide a chamber into which the marble was pushed to open the bottle. White's, by now the biggest soft drinks company in London and south-east England, featured a wide range of drinks on their price list in 1887, all of which were sold in Codd's glass bottles, with choices including strawberry soda, raspberry soda, cherryade and cream soda. In 1899, the first patent was issued for a glass-blowing machine for the automatic production of glass bottles. Earlier glass bottles had all been hand-blown. In America, soda fountains were initially more popular, and many Americans would frequent the soda fountain daily. Businessmen in Philadelphia and New York City also began selling soda water in the early 19th century. In the 1830s, John Matthews of New York City and John Lippincott of Philadelphia began manufacturing soda fountains. In The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, published in 1848, the caddish Huntingdon, recovering from months of debauchery, wakes at noon and gulps a bottle of soda-water.) In the early 20th century, sales of bottled soda increased greatly around the world, and in the second half of the 20th century, canned soft drinks became an important share of the market. Since then, soft drink vending machines have become increasingly popular. Annual average consumption in the United States, at 153.5 liters, was about twice that in the United Kingdom (77.7) or Canada (85.3).In recent years, soda consumption has generally declined in the West. At the same time, soda consumption has increased in some low- or middle-income countries such as Cameroon, Georgia, India and Vietnam as soda manufacturers increasingly target these markets and consumers have increasing discretionary income. Soft drinks can be made at home by mixing a syrup or dry ingredients with carbonated water, or by Lacto-fermentation. Syrups are commercially sold by companies such as Soda-Club; Carbonated water is made using a soda siphon or a home carbonation system or by dropping dry ice into water. This is not only the functional parameter (in other words, the level of the major constituent), but the level of impurities, the microbiological status, and physical parameters such as color, particle size, etc.Some soft drinks contain measurable amounts of alcohol. In the United States, soft drinks (as well as other products such as non-alcoholic beer) are allowed by law to contain up to 0.5% alcohol by volume. A small amount of alcohol is introduced in some soft drinks where alcohol is used in the preparation of the flavoring extracts such as vanilla extract. However, PepsiCo and the Coca-Cola Company remain the two largest producers of soft drinks in most regions of the world. A few experimental studies reported the role sugar-sweetened soft drinks potentially contribute to these ailments, though other studies show conflicting information. According to a 2013 systematic review of systematic reviews, 83.3% of the systematic reviews without reported conflict of interest concluded that sugar-sweetened soft drinks consumption could be a potential risk factor for weight gain. The consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages is associated with weight and obesity, and changes in consumption can help predict changes in weight.The consumption of sugar-sweetened soft drinks can also be associated with many weight-related diseases, including diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular risk factors. Most soft drinks contain high concentrations of simple carbohydrates: glucose, fructose, sucrose and other simple sugars. The risk would be greater if the frequency of consumption is high.A large number of soda pops are acidic as are many fruits, sauces, and other foods. It has also been suggested that brushing teeth right after drinking soft drinks should be avoided as this can result in additional erosion to the teeth due to mechanical action of the toothbrush on weakened enamel. A 2006 study of several thousand men and women, found that women who regularly drank cola-based sodas (three or more a day) had significantly lower bone mineral density (BMD) of about 4% in the hip compared to women who did not consume colas. In 2006, the United Kingdom Food Standards Agency published the results of its survey of benzene levels in soft drinks, which tested 150 products and found that four contained benzene levels above the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for drinking water. The United States Food and Drug Administration released its own test results of several soft drinks containing benzoates and ascorbic or erythorbic acid. As of 2006, the FDA stated its belief that "the levels of benzene found in soft drinks and other beverages to date do not pose a safety concern for consumers". A study published in the Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology in 2013 concluded that consumption of soft drinks was associated with a 23% higher risk of developing kidney stones. In a 2019 study, 451,743 people who had higher consumption of soft drinks (two or more a day) were associated with mortality, artificially sweetened drinks with cardiovascular diseases and sugar-sweetened drinks with digestive diseases. Since at least 2006, debate on whether high-calorie soft drink vending machines should be allowed in schools has been on the rise. Opponents of the soft drink vending machines believe that soft drinks are a significant contributor to childhood obesity and tooth decay, and that allowing soft drink sales in schools encourages children to believe they are safe to consume in moderate to large quantities. Opponents also argue that schools have a responsibility to look after the health of the children in their care, and that allowing children easy access to soft drinks violates that responsibility. Vending machine proponents believe that obesity is a complex issue and soft drinks are not the only cause. A 2011 bill to tax soft drinks in California failed, with some opposing lawmakers arguing that parents—not the government—should be responsible for children's drink choices.On May 3, 2006, the Alliance for a Healthier Generation, Cadbury Schweppes, the Coca-Cola Company, PepsiCo, and the American Beverage Association announced new guidelines that will voluntarily remove high-calorie soft drinks from all U.S. schools. Among a wide range of measures, from September 2006, school lunches will be free from carbonated drinks. Schools will also end the sale of junk food (including carbonated drinks) in vending machines and tuck shops. The article examines a school district's policy regarding limiting the sale and marketing of soda in public schools, and how certain policies can invoke a violation of the First Amendment. The act bans the selling of soft drinks to students and requires schools to provide healthier options such as water, unflavored low-fat milk, 100% fruit and vegetable drinks or sugar-free carbonated drinks. Proponents of the act predict the new mandate it will make it easier for students to make healthy drink choices while at school.In 2015, Terry-McElarth and colleagues published a study in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine on regular soda policies and their effect on school drink availability and student consumption. The study analyzed state- and school district-level policies mandating soda bans and found that state bans were associated with significantly lower school soda availability but district bans showed no significant associations. Among student populations, state policy was directly associated with significantly lower school soda availability and indirectly associated with lower student consumption. In the United States, legislators, health experts and consumer advocates are considering levying higher taxes on the sale of soft drinks and other sweetened products to help curb the epidemic of obesity among Americans, and its harmful impact on overall health. Others say that taxes should help fund education to increase consumer awareness of the unhealthy effects of excessive soft drink consumption, and also help cover costs of caring for conditions resulting from overconsumption. The food and drink industry holds considerable clout in Washington, DC, as it has contributed more than $50 million to legislators since 2000.In January 2013, a British lobby group called for the price of sugary fizzy drinks to be increased, with the money raised (an estimated £1 billion at 20p per litre) to be put towards a "Children's Future Fund", overseen by an independent body, which would encourage children to eat healthily in school.In 2017, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and the Kingdom of Bahrain imposed a 50% tax on soft drinks and a 100% tax on energy drinks to curb excess consumption of the commodity and for additional revenue. In March 2013, New York City's mayor Michael Bloomberg proposed to ban the sale of non-diet soft drinks larger than 16 ounces, except in convenience stores and supermarkets.

**Summary of Source Content on Beverages**

**Schorle (German Beverage)**
Schorle is a German drink made by diluting juice or wine with carbonated water or lemonade. The most common type is Apfelschorle (apple juice and sparkling water). It is widely sold in bottles. Dilution makes it less sweet or alcoholic, suitable as a summer refreshment or beer alternative. Typical proportions are half juice/wine and half carbonated water, though in the Palatinate region a "fett" (fat) wine schorle uses considerably less water. There is no direct English equivalent, though "spritzer" is similar; Schorle is typically freshly mixed, not pre-bottled like some spritzers. Related terms include Gespritzter (Austria/Germany) and Spritzer.

Varieties are defined by the mixer: wine with mineral water (sour Schorle/Sauergespritzter), wine with lemonade (sweet Schorle/Arbeitersekt), wine with cola (Cola-Schoppen, in Austria red/white Cola), and juice with mineral water (Juice-Schorle/Fruit-Schorle; in Austria spritzed apple/orange juice). The German article for Schorle varies regionally (die, das, der). Mixing proportions are roughly 1:1, but juice Schorle often has more water.

Etymology: The term likely originates from "Schorlemorle" (first "Schurlemurle" in 18th-century Lower Bavaria) for wine mixed with sparkling water. Possible origins include: a play on words; Southern German "schuren" (to bubble/fizz); Dutch "schorriemorrie" (ragtag); or Persian-Turkish "schurmur" (confusion), which entered European languages.

**Mixing with Wine**
*   **Germany:** Weinschorle (wine spritzer) uses wines like Riesling, Blauer Portugieser, Müller-Thurgau. "Sour" = with carbonated water; "sweet" = with lemonade; "sweet and sour" = with both. In the Palatinate, the wine ratio is often much higher, served in a 0.5L "Dubbeglas." Wine mixed with cola is called red/white cola.
*   **Regional Terms:** In Hesse, "Gespritzer" is a 2:1 or 3:1 mix of apple wine and sparkling water (Sauergespritzter vs. Süßgespritzter with lemonade). In Rheinhessen, it's wine with sparkling water, cola, or lemonade. In Bavaria and Austria, "Gespritzter" is similar.
*   **Austria:** By regulation, a "G'spritzter"/"Gespritzter"/"Spritzer" must contain ≥50% wine and ≤50% soda/mineral water, with ≥4.5% alcohol. "Schorle" is uncommon. Colloquial terms: "Sommerspritzer" (less wine), "Winterspritzer" (more wine). Typically made with table wines like Grüner Veltliner or Zweigelt, served in 0.25L stemware or 0.4-0.5L beer mugs. Sweet versions use herbal lemonade (e.g., Almdudler, called Almweiß, Liftler, Tiroler). "Kaiserspritzer" includes elderflower syrup. Regional names: "Sprüher"/"Sprühwein" (Vienna), "Siphon" (Lower Austria), "Mischung" (Styria). In Vorarlberg, terms like "white-sour" describe the mix; "Gespritzter" is understood but rarely used. In eastern Austria, "Gespritzter" can be a derogatory term for a person.
*   **Switzerland:** "Gespritzter" is white wine with mineral water (sauer) or lemonade (süß).
*   **Other Countries:** Similar drinks exist: "fröccs" in Hungary; "Spritz"/"Spriz"/"Spriss(eto)" in Italy (from Austrian influence); "špricer"/"gemišt" in former Yugoslavia (red wine with cola/lemonade called "Bambus" in Croatia); "Tinto de verano" (red wine & lemonade) in Spain; "kalimotxo" (red wine & cola) in Basque country; "spritzer" in Great Britain (since 1980s); "wine coolers" in the United States.

**Mixing with Juice**
"Fruit schorle" mixes carbonated water and fruit juice. Bottled versions are popular. Water-to-juice proportion varies but is typically under 50% juice, often 40-60%. Apfelschorle is very popular; it works with sour/bitter fruits (e.g., grapefruit) or sweet ones (e.g., cherry). It contains less energy than pure juice. Commercially, apple schorlen have 55-60% fruit content, 5-6g fructose, sometimes with synthetic flavoring. Apfelschorle is also drunk as a sports drink for minerals and carbohydrates, being nearly isotonic.

**Grape Soda**
Grape drinks (grape soda, pop, purple drink in U.S. regions) are sweetened, grape-flavored, deep purple drinks, carbonated (e.g., Fanta) or non-carbonated (e.g., Kool-Aid). Grapeade appeared in late 19th-century American soda fountains (brands: Miner's, Lash's). Modern commercial grape sodas use artificial flavorings like methyl anthranilate (simulating Concord grapes) and food coloring. Hard grape sodas exist (e.g., Henry's Hard Soda). Non-alcoholic grape soda is used in cocktails.

**Tampico Beverages**
An American manufacturer of bottled fruit-flavored drinks and gelatin, owned by Houchens Industries Inc. since 2008. Founded 1989 with Citrus Punch. By early 1990s, first international licensee in Mexico. By 2014, its Citrus Gallon was the top-selling item in U.S. refrigerated drinks. It provides concentrate to licensees in over 50 countries. U.S. products are labeled as "punch"; they consist mainly of water, sugar, and flavoring, with tiny fruit juice proportions.

**Ceylon Cold Stores (Elephant House)**
A Sri Lankan company producing carbonated drinks, ice cream, processed meats. Market leader in Sri Lanka despite global competition.
*   **History:** Founded 1866 as Colombo Ice Company, importing Sri Lanka's first ice-making machine (1863). Initial capital £1,900, 22 employees. First premises in Slave Island, known as 'Ice Kompaniya'. German engineer Arthur Kurt Von Possner (first manager) introduced aerated water with "Elephant" trademark, later "Elephant House". Early drinks: soda and lemonade, award-winning at international fairs.
*   **Acquisitions/Expansions:** 1880: Acquired J. Maitland's medical hall business (company later liquidated). 1894: Syndicate led by Tom Walker bought assets, formed New Colombo Ice Company. 1910: Bought Galle Face Ice Company for Rs. 45,000. 1919: Acquired Von Possner's British Aerated and Mineral Water Company for Rs. 175,000. 1923: New ice plant. 1925: Built cold storage. 1928: Opened Colombo cold stores; bought Pure Ice and Aerated Waters Manufactory. 1932: Acquired Ceylon Creameries Limited for milk/ice cream. 1934: Bought Ceylon Ice and Cold Storage Company for Rs. 850,000. 1935: Installed carbonic acid gas plant. Also produced bread.
*   **Modern Era:** 1941: Renamed Ceylon Cold Stores Limited. 1964: First Ceylonese chairman, Mallory Wijesinghe. 1970: Listed on Colombo Stock Exchange. 1991: Came under John Keells Holdings (54% shareholding) via Whittalls Group acquisition. 1998: Modern bottling plant at Kaduwela. 2007: John Keells invested ~Rs. 1 billion in new factory line.

**Faygo**
Soft drink company headquartered in Detroit, Michigan, a subsidiary of National Beverage Corp. Founded November 1907 as Feigenson Brothers Bottle Works by Russian immigrant bakers Ben and Perry Feigenson. Original flavors (fruit punch, strawberry, grape) based on cake frosting recipes. Early delivery by horse-drawn wagon.
*   **Growth:** Next decade: purchased houses, hired first employee, added flavors (Sassafras Soda, Lithiated Lemon), built new plant. 1921: Shortened name to Faygo. 1922: First delivery truck. 1920s new flavors: vanilla soft drink, seltzer, "Ace Hi", Rock & Rye. 1935: Opened current Gratiot Avenue plant. Briefly produced beer. Mid-1940s: Brothers turned company over to sons.
*   **Marketing:** 1956: "Faygo Kid" cowboy ads. Jim Henson's Muppets ads for strawberry soda with Wilkins and Wontkins.
*   **Expansion:** Initially sold only in Michigan due to shelf life; chemists later installed water filtration to solve this. 1960s: Ads on Detroit Tigers broadcasts expanded regional popularity; unable to cancel ads, shipped to wholesalers' warehouses. Sales rose from $6 million (1966) to $20.4 million (1971). 1970s ads: "Faygo Boat Song" on Boblo Boat.
*   **Product Lines:** 1960s: Introduced low-calorie "Ohana" line (became majority of sales). 1961: Launched "Royal Line" premium; first run of Royal Hawaiian Pineapple Orange had unsterilized juice causing exploding bottles, recalled, Dole provided replacement juice. Six other 1960s flavors added. Original strawberry renamed "Redpop" late 1960s.
*   **Challenges:** 1978 Michigan container deposit law: Faygo incorrectly bet on returnable cans over glass, hurting profits during switch back.
*   **Ownership Changes:** 1986: Sold to TreeSweet Products Corp. for $105 million. 1987: Sold to National Beverage Corp.
*   **Later Products:** 1980s: Flavored carbonated water. 1996: Non-carbonated "Ohana" line (punches, iced tea, lemonade). 2007: 100th anniversary, new "Centennial Soda" flavor from contest. March 2014: Introduced ginger ale "Faygo Gold".
*   **Reception:** Ranked best-tasting American root beer by Bon Appétit (September 2009).
*   **Pop Culture:** Detroit hip hop group Insane Clown Posse references it and sprays audiences with "Faygo showers".

**Yoo-hoo**
American chocolate-flavored beverage created by Natale Olivieri in Garfield, New Jersey, 1928. Currently made by Keurig Dr Pepper. As of 2019, primarily water, high-fructose corn syrup, whey.
*   **History:** Olivieri bottled carbonated fruit drinks mid-1920s; adapted home canning heat processing to prevent chocolate drink spoilage, began bottling pasteurized Yoo-hoo 1928. 1940s: Thomas Giresi opened bottling plant in Batesburg, South Carolina. 1960s: Ad campaign with Yogi Berra and Yankees.
*   **Ownership:** 1950s-1976: Owned by BBC Industries. 1976: Sold to Iroquois Brands. 1981: Sold to private investors. 1989: Sold to Pernod Ricard. 2001: Sold to Cadbury Schweppes (production by Mott's, marketing by Snapple). May 2008: Cadbury-Schweppes split, Yoo-hoo went to Dr Pepper Snapple Group.
*   **Operations:** Headquarters Tarrytown, New York; plants in Carlstadt, NJ, and Aspers, PA; Opelousas, LA plant closed 2009. Once owned other chocolate milk brands (Choc-Ola, Brownie, Cocoa Dusty, Chocolate Soldier).
*   **Lawsuit:** 2010: Timothy Dahl sued Dr Pepper Snapple Group for misleading advertising, alleging Yoo-hoo contained partially hydrogenated oil, mostly water/sugars/chemicals, virtually no milk. Mott's stated it contained seven vitamins/minerals, no preservatives.
*   **Papal Anecdote:** During a papal visit to Denver, sources reported Pope John Paul II liked Yoo-hoo; Vatican later denied any specific preference.
*   **Ingredients (Early Feb 2019):** Water, high fructose corn syrup, whey, <2% of: cocoa (alkali process), nonfat dry milk, natural/artificial flavors, sodium caseinate, corn syrup solids, calcium phosphate, dipotassium phosphate, palm oil, guar gum, xanthan gum, mono and diglycerides, salt, spice, soy lecithin, niacinamide (B3), sucralose, vitamin A palmitate, riboflavin (B2), vitamin D3.
*   **Pop Culture:** Dec 2022: Musician Ye on InfoWars used bottle to mock Benjamin Netanyahu.
*   **Flavors:** New flavors introduced 1995: chocolate-coconut, -mint, -banana, -strawberry. Others: vanilla, strawberry, cookies & cream, chocolate peanut butter, chocolate caramel. Discontinued: Double Fudge, banana, Island Coconut.

**Banta (Banta Soda/Goli Soda/Goti Soda/Fotash Jawl)**
Popular carbonated lemon/orange-flavored soft drink in India since late 19th century, sold in iconic Codd-neck bottle sealed by a glass marble. Opening by pressing marble is considered fun. Sold by street-sellers (bantawallahs) at ₹5–₹30, served in glass tumblers, plastic cups, formerly kulhars (earthen pots). Part of Indian popular culture. High demand in April-May summer, often mixed with lemon juice, crushed ice, chaat masala, kala namak (black salt) as carbonated shikanjvi/jal-jeera variant. Popular in Delhi, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh; "Panneer Soda" (with rose essence) popular in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh. In Delhi, known as "Delhi's local drink", popular in Old Delhi and university campuses. Pandit Ved Prakash Lemon Wale in Chandni Chowk selling since 1870s. Also available in fancy bars, mass-manufactured versions in cafes/bars/hotels.
*   **Etymology:** Named after marble: Hindi/Punjabi "banta", "goli", "goti", "kancha". Also called "kanchay waali drink" or "nimbu soda" in Delhi. Bengali: "Fotash Jawl".
*   **History:** Codd-neck bottle invented by Hiram Codd, patented 1872. Now produced only in India (for banta) and Japan (for ramune). Children often broke bottles to get marbles, making old bottles collector's items. Pre-independence, bottles imported from Britain; banned in some cities during independence movement as freedom fighters used them with chuna (calcium hydroxide) for improvised cannons. 1950s: Sold from horse-drawn carts with soda-making equipment.
*   **Production:** Ingredients (salt, water, flavors from fruit juice or commercial flavors) poured into bottle via funnel, then carbonated in a machine infusing CO2, sealing marble against gasket. Bottles are reusable, collected, cleaned, refilled.
*   **Present-Day:** Sole Indian manufacturer of Codd-neck bottles is Khandelwal Glass Works (Sasni, Uttar Pradesh) since 1981; competitor Mahalakshmi Glass Works (Hyderabad) closed. Sales peaked early 1990s (100,000 bags/year, 75 bottles/bag) before Pepsi/Coca-Cola re-entry 1993; by 2010 sales dropped nearly half.
*   **Bottling:** Uses flavoring agent Lemon No. 1 by IFF. Largely bottled by unorganized manufacturers (price as low as ₹2). 2017: Delhi had over 100 single-room bottling units. Chennai had 150 unorganized units in 1970s, down to 50 by 2018. Kozzmo Beverages (Chennai, started 2018) makes FSSAI-certified hygienic prepackaged goli soda in 6 flavors. Spark Premium Codd Soda introduced first premium branded goli soda in Telangana (2019); manufacturer cited traditional filling as cumbersome, semi-automatic machines enabled comeback.

**Codd-neck Bottle**
Bottle for carbonated drinks with closure using a glass marble held against a rubber seal in the neck. Designed and patented 1872 by Hiram Codd of London. Thick glass withstands pressure. Filled upside down; gas pressure forces marble against washer to seal. Neck pinched to provide chamber for marble when opening. Extremely popular in soft drink/brewing industries in Europe, India, Australasia. Declined after introduction of steel crown cork. Vintage bottles are collector's items; cobalt-colored ones can fetch thousands of pounds. Still used for Japanese Ramune and Indian Banta. (Note: Etymology linking "codswallop" to Codd bottles is generally dismissed.)

**Carbonated Drinks (Soft Drinks)**
Water-based flavored drink, usually carbonated, with added sweetener (sugar, high-fructose corn syrup, fruit juice, sugar substitute). Can contain caffeine, colorings, preservatives. "Soft" contrasts with "hard" alcoholic drinks; must contain <0.5% alcohol by volume in many places to be considered non-alcoholic. Types include lemon-lime, orange soda, cola, grape soda, ginger ale, root beer. Served cold/over ice/room temperature in various containers (cans, glass/plastic bottles). Available widely in restaurants, stores, vending machines, soda fountains.
*   **Terminology:** Industry category "soft drink". Regional names: pop, cool drink, fizzy drink, cola, soda, soda pop, carbonated drink, cold drink, fizzy juice, lolly water, seltzer, coke, tonic, mineral, sugary drinks. U.S. 2003 Harvard Dialect Survey: "soda" dominant in Northeast, California, Milwaukee/St. Louis; "pop" in Midwest/Pacific Northwest (25%); "coke" in South (12%); "tonic" in eastern Massachusetts (declining). Canada: "pop" prevalent; "soft drink" common in Montreal English. UK/Ireland: "fizzy drink"; "pop"/"fizzy pop" in Northern England, South Wales, Midlands; "mineral" in Ireland; Scotland: "fizzy juice"/"juice"/"ginger". Australia/New Zealand: "soft drink"/"fizzy drink". South Africa: "cool drink". UK calls 7-Up/Sprite "lemonade". Other languages use descriptive or prototypical names (e.g., Czech "limonáda" for all, Slovak "malinovka" for all).
*   **History:** Origins in medieval Middle Eastern fruit-flavored drinks (sharbat) sweetened with sugar/syrup/honey. In Tudor England: 'water imperial' (lemon, cream of tartar), 'Manays Cryste' (rosewater/violets/cinnamon). Lemonade (water, lemon juice, honey, no carbonation) existed; Parisian Compagnie des Limonadiers had monopoly from 1676.
*   **Carbonation:** Carbonated drinks consist mainly of carbonated water; CO2 dissolution causes fizz. Carbonation levels up to 5 volumes CO2 per liquid volume; ginger ale/colas ~3.5 volumes.
*   **Invention/Development:** 1767: Joseph Priestley discovered method to infuse water with CO2 at a Leeds brewery. 1772: Published paper on making carbonated water. John Mervin Nooth improved design for commercial pharmacy use. Torbern Bergman invented apparatus for large-scale imitation mineral water. Jöns Jacob Berzelius added flavors late 18th century. Thomas Henry sold artificial mineral water medicinally from 1770s. Johann Jacob Schweppe founded Schweppes 1783 in Geneva, moved to London 1792, commercialized Malvern Water 1843, received royal warrant.
*   **Flavored Carbonated Drinks:** Early 1800s: flavoring combined with carbonated water; earliest reference to carbonated ginger beer 1809. Pharmacists added herbs/chemicals (birch bark, dandelion, sarsaparilla, fruit extracts).
*   **Phosphate Soda:** U.S. variant late 1870s, popular 1900-1930s. Consists of 1 oz fruit syrup, 1/2 tsp phosphoric acid, carbonated water/ice.
*   **Mass Market/Industrialization:** By 1840s, over 50 manufacturers in London (10 in 1820s). Carbonated lemonade available at British stalls 1833. R. White's Lemonade launched 1845. 1851 Great Exhibition: Schweppes official supplier, sold over million bottles. Tonic water invented 1858 (quinine, soda, sugar for malaria prophylaxis in British colonies); gin and tonic originated in British India. Bottle sealing problem: Hiram Codd invented Codd-neck bottle 1870 (marble/rubber washer seal). R. White's 1887 price list featured many drinks in Codd bottles. 1892: William Painter patented Crown Cork Bottle Seal. 1899: First patent for automatic glass bottle-blowing machine; by 1903, production rose to ~58,000 bottles/day. In America, soda fountains were initially popular (Benjamin Silliman sold soda water 1806 in New Haven). Bottled drinks grew slowly due to U.S. glass industry issues. Early 20th century: bottled soda sales increased worldwide. 1920s: "Home-Paks" (six-pack cartons) invented; vending machines appeared. Second half 20th century: canned soft drinks became significant.
*   **Consumption:** Per capita consumption varies globally. 2014 top countries: Argentina, United States, Chile, Mexico. U.S. annual average 153.5 liters, about double UK (77.7) or Canada (85.3). In recent years, soda consumption declined in West: U.S. peak 1998, then fell; study found proportion of Americans drinking sugary beverage daily fell from ~62% to 50% for adults, 80% to 61% for children (2003-2014). Increased in some low/middle-income countries (Cameroon, Georgia, India, Vietnam).
*   **Production:** Mixing dry/fresh ingredients with water at factories or home (using syrup/dry ingredients with carbonated water, or lacto-fermentation). Carbonated water made with siphon, home carbonation, dry ice, or food-grade CO2 (often from ammonia plants). Drinks like ginger ale/root beer often brewed with yeast. Ingredients must meet specifications (function, impurities, microbiology, color, particle size). Some soft drinks contain small alcohol amounts (<0.5% ABV in U.S.), possibly from natural fermentation in old methods or flavoring extracts.
*   **Producers:** Market control varies by country. Largest globally: PepsiCo and Coca-Cola Company. In North America, Keurig Dr Pepper and Jones Soda also have significant share.
*   **Health Concerns:** Over-consumption associated with obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, dental caries, low nutrient levels. 2013 systematic review: 83.3% of reviews without conflict of interest linked sugar-sweetened soft drinks to weight gain risk.
    *   **Obesity:** U.S. sweetened beverage consumption doubled 1977-2002, paralleling obesity doubling. Associated with weight, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular risks.
    *   **Dental Decay:** High simple carbohydrates fermented by oral bacteria produce acids eroding enamel. Acidity also contributes; some flavored sparkling waters as erosive as orange juice (2007 study). Using straw reduces contact; brushing immediately after drinking not advised.
    *   **Bone Density:** 2006 study: women drinking ≥3 cola-based sodas daily had ~4% lower hip bone mineral density vs. non-consumers; not significant in men.
    *   **Benzene:** 2006 UK survey found 4/150 products above WHO drinking water guidelines. 2006 FDA tests found 5 drinks above EPA 5 ppb standard but stated no safety concern.
    *   **Kidney Stones:** 2013 study: soft drink consumption associated with 23% higher risk.
    *   **Mortality/Disease:** 2019 study of 451,743 people: ≥2 soft drinks daily associated with mortality; artificially sweetened with cardiovascular diseases; sugar-sweetened with digestive diseases.
*   **Government Regulation:**
    *   **Schools:** Debate over vending machines in schools due to childhood obesity/tooth decay concerns. May 3, 2006: Alliance for a Healthier Generation, beverage companies (Cadbury Schweppes, Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, American Beverage Association) announced voluntary removal of high-calorie soft drinks from U.S. schools. May 19, 2006: UK banned carbonated drinks from school lunches and sales in vending machines/tuck shops from September 2006. 2008 article discussed First Amendment implications of restricting marketing in schools; commercial speech protected, but contracts can restrict sales. Dec 13, 2010: President Obama signed Healthy Hunger-Free Kids Act (effective 2014) banning soft drink sales in federally funded schools, requiring healthy options (water, unflavored low-fat milk, 100% fruit/vegetable drinks, sugar-free carbonated drinks). Portion sizes: 8 oz (elementary), 12 oz (middle/high). 2015 study found state-level soda bans in schools associated with lower soda availability and indirectly lower student consumption for some populations.
    *   **Taxation:** U.S. considered higher taxes to curb obesity. British lobby group (2013) called for price increase on sugary fizzy drinks to fund "Children's Future Fund". 2017: Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain imposed 50% tax on soft drinks, 100% on energy drinks.
    *   **Attempted Ban:** March 2013: NYC Mayor Michael Bloomberg proposed ban on sale of non-diet soft drinks >16 oz (exempting convenience stores/supermarkets). Lawsuit overturned ban as "arbitrary and capricious"; appellate courts upheld, ban unenforceable as of 2021.

Introduction and Background
Task-oriented dialogue systems are primarily designed to search and interact with large databases which contain information pertaining to a certain dialogue domain: the main purpose of such systems is to assist the users in accomplishing a well-defined task such as flight booking BIBREF0, tourist information BIBREF1, restaurant search BIBREF2, or booking a taxi BIBREF3. These systems are typically constructed around rigid task-specific ontologies BIBREF1, BIBREF4 which enumerate the constraints the users can express using a collection of slots (e.g., price range for restaurant search) and their slot values (e.g., cheap, expensive for the aforementioned slots). Conversations are then modelled as a sequence of actions that constrain slots to particular values. This explicit semantic space is manually engineered by the system designer. It serves as the output of the natural language understanding component as well as the input to the language generation component both in traditional modular systems BIBREF5, BIBREF6 and in more recent end-to-end task-oriented dialogue systems BIBREF7, BIBREF8, BIBREF9, BIBREF3.
Working with such explicit semantics for task-oriented dialogue systems poses several critical challenges on top of the manual time-consuming domain ontology design. First, it is difficult to collect domain-specific data labelled with explicit semantic representations. As a consequence, despite recent data collection efforts to enable training of task-oriented systems across multiple domains BIBREF0, BIBREF3, annotated datasets are still few and far between, as well as limited in size and the number of domains covered. Second, the current approach constrains the types of dialogue the system can support, resulting in artificial conversations, and breakdowns when the user does not understand what the system can and cannot support. In other words, training a task-based dialogue system for voice-controlled search in a new domain always implies the complex, expensive, and time-consuming process of collecting and annotating sufficient amounts of in-domain dialogue data.
In this paper, we present a demo system based on an alternative approach to task-oriented dialogue. Relying on non-generative response retrieval we describe the PolyResponse conversational search engine and its application in the task of restaurant search and booking. The engine is trained on hundreds of millions of real conversations from a general domain (i.e., Reddit), using an implicit representation of semantics that directly optimizes the task at hand. It learns what responses are appropriate in different conversational contexts, and consequently ranks a large pool of responses according to their relevance to the current user utterance and previous dialogue history (i.e., dialogue context).
The technical aspects of the underlying conversational search engine are explained in detail in our recent work BIBREF11, while the details concerning the Reddit training data are also available in another recent publication BIBREF12. In this demo, we put focus on the actual practical usefulness of the search engine by demonstrating its potential in the task of restaurant search, and extending it to deal with multi-modal data. We describe a PolyReponse system that assists the users in finding a relevant restaurant according to their preference, and then additionally helps them to make a booking in the selected restaurant. Due to its retrieval-based design, with the PolyResponse engine there is no need to engineer a structured ontology, or to solve the difficult task of general language generation. This design also bypasses the construction of dedicated decision-making policy modules. The large ranking model already encapsulates a lot of knowledge about natural language and conversational flow.
Since retrieved system responses are presented visually to the user, the PolyResponse restaurant search engine is able to combine text responses with relevant visual information (e.g., photos from social media associated with the current restaurant and related to the user utterance), effectively yielding a multi-modal response. This setup of using voice as input, and responding visually is becoming more and more prevalent with the rise of smart screens like Echo Show and even mixed reality. Finally, the PolyResponse restaurant search engine is multilingual: it is currently deployed in 8 languages enabling search over restaurants in 8 cities around the world. System snapshots in four different languages are presented in Figure FIGREF16, while screencast videos that illustrate the dialogue flow with the PolyResponse engine are available at: https://tinyurl.com/y3evkcfz.
PolyResponse: Conversational Search
The PolyResponse system is powered by a single large conversational search engine, trained on a large amount of conversational and image data, as shown in Figure FIGREF2. In simple words, it is a ranking model that learns to score conversational replies and images in a given conversational context. The highest-scoring responses are then retrieved as system outputs. The system computes two sets of similarity scores: 1) $S(r,c)$ is the score of a candidate reply $r$ given a conversational context $c$, and 2) $S(p,c)$ is the score of a candidate photo $p$ given a conversational context $c$. These scores are computed as a scaled cosine similarity of a vector that represents the context ($h_c$), and a vector that represents the candidate response: a text reply ($h_r$) or a photo ($h_p$). For instance, $S(r,c)$ is computed as $S(r,c)=C cos(h_r,h_c)$, where $C$ is a learned constant. The part of the model dealing with text input (i.e., obtaining the encodings $h_c$ and $h_r$) follows the architecture introduced recently by Henderson:2019acl. We provide only a brief recap here; see the original paper for further details.
PolyResponse: Conversational Search ::: Text Representation.
The model, implemented as a deep neural network, learns to respond by training on hundreds of millions context-reply $(c,r)$ pairs. First, similar to Henderson:2017arxiv, raw text from both $c$ and $r$ is converted to unigrams and bigrams. All input text is first lower-cased and tokenised, numbers with 5 or more digits get their digits replaced by a wildcard symbol #, while words longer than 16 characters are replaced by a wildcard token LONGWORD. Sentence boundary tokens are added to each sentence. The vocabulary consists of the unigrams that occur at least 10 times in a random 10M subset of the Reddit training set (see Figure FIGREF2) plus the 200K most frequent bigrams in the same random subset.
During training, we obtain $d$-dimensional feature representations ($d=320$) shared between contexts and replies for each unigram and bigram jointly with other neural net parameters. A state-of-the-art architecture based on transformers BIBREF13 is then applied to unigram and bigram vectors separately, which are then averaged to form the final 320-dimensional encoding. That encoding is then passed through three fully-connected non-linear hidden layers of dimensionality $1,024$. The final layer is linear and maps the text into the final $l$-dimensional ($l=512$) representation: $h_c$ and $h_r$. Other standard and more sophisticated encoder models can also be used to provide final encodings $h_c$ and $h_r$, but the current architecture shows a good trade-off between speed and efficacy with strong and robust performance in our empirical evaluations on the response retrieval task using Reddit BIBREF14, OpenSubtitles BIBREF15, and AmazonQA BIBREF16 conversational test data, see BIBREF12 for further details.
In training the constant $C$ is constrained to lie between 0 and $\sqrt{l}$. Following Henderson:2017arxiv, the scoring function in the training objective aims to maximise the similarity score of context-reply pairs that go together, while minimising the score of random pairings: negative examples. Training proceeds via SGD with batches comprising 500 pairs (1 positive and 499 negatives).
PolyResponse: Conversational Search ::: Photo Representation.
Photos are represented using convolutional neural net (CNN) models pretrained on ImageNet BIBREF17. We use a MobileNet model with a depth multiplier of 1.4, and an input dimension of $224 \times 224$ pixels as in BIBREF18. This provides a $1,280 \times 1.4 = 1,792$-dimensional representation of a photo, which is then passed through a single hidden layer of dimensionality $1,024$ with ReLU activation, before being passed to a hidden layer of dimensionality 512 with no activation to provide the final representation $h_p$.
PolyResponse: Conversational Search ::: Data Source 1: Reddit.
For training text representations we use a Reddit dataset similar to AlRfou:2016arxiv. Our dataset is large and provides natural conversational structure: all Reddit data from January 2015 to December 2018, available as a public BigQuery dataset, span almost 3.7B comments BIBREF12. We preprocess the dataset to remove uninformative and long comments by retaining only sentences containing more than 8 and less than 128 word tokens. After pairing all comments/contexts $c$ with their replies $r$, we obtain more than 727M context-reply $(c,r)$ pairs for training, see Figure FIGREF2.
PolyResponse: Conversational Search ::: Data Source 2: Yelp.
Once the text encoding sub-networks are trained, a photo encoder is learned on top of a pretrained MobileNet CNN, using data taken from the Yelp Open dataset: it contains around 200K photos and their captions. Training of the multi-modal sub-network then maximises the similarity of captions encoded with the response encoder $h_r$ to the photo representation $h_p$. As a result, we can compute the score of a photo given a context using the cosine similarity of the respective vectors. A photo will be scored highly if it looks like its caption would be a good response to the current context.
PolyResponse: Conversational Search ::: Index of Responses.
The Yelp dataset is used at inference time to provide text and photo candidates to display to the user at each step in the conversation. Our restaurant search is currently deployed separately for each city, and we limit the responses to a given city. For instance, for our English system for Edinburgh we work with 396 restaurants, 4,225 photos (these include additional photos obtained using the Google Places API without captions), 6,725 responses created from the structured information about restaurants that Yelp provides, converted using simple templates to sentences of the form such as “Restaurant X accepts credit cards.”, 125,830 sentences extracted from online reviews.
PolyResponse: Conversational Search ::: PolyResponse in a Nutshell.
The system jointly trains two encoding functions (with shared word embeddings) $f(context)$ and $g(reply)$ which produce encodings $h_c$ and $h_r$, so that the similarity $S(c,r)$ is high for all $(c,r)$ pairs from the Reddit training data and low for random pairs. The encoding function $g()$ is then frozen, and an encoding function $t(photo)$ is learnt which makes the similarity between a photo and its associated caption high for all (photo, caption) pairs from the Yelp dataset, and low for random pairs. $t$ is a CNN pretrained on ImageNet, with a shallow one-layer DNN on top. Given a new context/query, we then provide its encoding $h_c$ by applying $f()$, and find plausible text replies and photo responses according to functions $g()$ and $t()$, respectively. These should be responses that look like answers to the query, and photos that look like they would have captions that would be answers to the provided query.
At inference, finding relevant candidates given a context reduces to computing $h_c$ for the context $c$ , and finding nearby $h_r$ and $h_p$ vectors. The response vectors can all be pre-computed, and the nearest neighbour search can be further optimised using standard libraries such as Faiss BIBREF19 or approximate nearest neighbour retrieval BIBREF20, giving an efficient search that scales to billions of candidate responses.
The system offers both voice and text input and output. Speech-to-text and text-to-speech conversion in the PolyResponse system is currently supported by the off-the-shelf Google Cloud tools.
Dialogue Flow
The ranking model lends itself to the one-shot task of finding the most relevant responses in a given context. However, a restaurant-browsing system needs to support a dialogue flow where the user finds a restaurant, and then asks questions about it. The dialogue state for each search scenario is represented as the set of restaurants that are considered relevant. This starts off as all the restaurants in the given city, and is assumed to monotonically decrease in size as the conversation progresses until the user converges to a single restaurant. A restaurant is only considered valid in the context of a new user input if it has relevant responses corresponding to it. This flow is summarised here:
S1. Initialise $R$ as the set of all restaurants in the city. Given the user's input, rank all the responses in the response pool pertaining to restaurants in $R$.
S2. Retrieve the top $N$ responses $r_1, r_2, \ldots , r_N$ with corresponding (sorted) cosine similarity scores: $s_1 \ge s_2 \ge \ldots \ge s_N$.
S3. Compute probability scores $p_i \propto \exp (a \cdot s_i)$ with $\sum _{i=1}^N p_i$, where $a>0$ is a tunable constant.
S4. Compute a score $q_e$ for each restaurant/entity $e \in R$, $q_e = \sum _{i: r_i \in e} p_i$.
S5. Update $R$ to the smallest set of restaurants with highest $q$ whose $q$-values sum up to more than a predefined threshold $t$.
S6. Display the most relevant responses associated with the updated $R$, and return to S2.
If there are multiple relevant restaurants, one response is shown from each. When only one restaurant is relevant, the top $N$ responses are all shown, and relevant photos are also displayed. The system does not require dedicated understanding, decision-making, and generation modules, and this dialogue flow does not rely on explicit task-tailored semantics. The set of relevant restaurants is kept internally while the system narrows it down across multiple dialogue turns. A simple set of predefined rules is used to provide a templatic spoken system response: e.g., an example rule is “One review of $e$ said $r$”, where $e$ refers to the restaurant, and $r$ to a relevant response associated with $e$. Note that while the demo is currently focused on the restaurant search task, the described “narrowing down” dialogue flow is generic and applicable to a variety of applications dealing with similar entity search.
The system can use a set of intent classifiers to allow resetting the dialogue state, or to activate the separate restaurant booking dialogue flow. These classifiers are briefly discussed in §SECREF4.
Other Functionality ::: Multilinguality.
The PolyResponse restaurant search is currently available in 8 languages and for 8 cities around the world: English (Edinburgh), German (Berlin), Spanish (Madrid), Mandarin (Taipei), Polish (Warsaw), Russian (Moscow), Korean (Seoul), and Serbian (Belgrade). Selected snapshots are shown in Figure FIGREF16, while we also provide videos demonstrating the use and behaviour of the systems at: https://tinyurl.com/y3evkcfz. A simple MT-based translate-to-source approach at inference time is currently used to enable the deployment of the system in other languages: 1) the pool of responses in each language is translated to English by Google Translate beforehand, and pre-computed encodings of their English translations are used as representations of each foreign language response; 2) a provided user utterance (i.e., context) is translated to English on-the-fly and its encoding $h_c$ is then learned. We plan to experiment with more sophisticated multilingual models in future work.
Other Functionality ::: Voice-Controlled Menu Search.
An additional functionality enables the user to get parts of the restaurant menu relevant to the current user utterance as responses. This is achieved by performing an additional ranking step of available menu items and retrieving the ones that are semantically relevant to the user utterance using exactly the same methodology as with ranking other responses. An example of this functionality is shown in Figure FIGREF21.
Other Functionality ::: Resetting and Switching to Booking.
The restaurant search system needs to support the discrete actions of restarting the conversation (i.e., resetting the set $R$), and should enable transferring to the slot-based table booking flow. This is achieved using two binary intent classifiers, that are run at each step in the dialogue. These classifiers make use of the already-computed $h_c$ vector that represents the user's latest text. A single-layer neural net is learned on top of the 512-dimensional encoding, with a ReLU activation and 100 hidden nodes. To train the classifiers, sets of 20 relevant paraphrases (e.g., “Start again”) are provided as positive examples. Finally, when the system successfully switches to the booking scenario, it proceeds to the slot filling task: it aims to extract all the relevant booking information from the user (e.g., date, time, number of people to dine). The entire flow of the system illustrating both the search phase and the booking phase is provided as the supplemental video material.
Conclusion and Future Work
This paper has presented a general approach to search-based dialogue that does not rely on explicit semantic representations such as dialogue acts or slot-value ontologies, and allows for multi-modal responses. In future work, we will extend the current demo system to more tasks and languages, and work with more sophisticated encoders and ranking functions. Besides the initial dialogue flow from this work (§SECREF3), we will also work with more complex flows dealing, e.g., with user intent shifts.
Head–tail
Introduction and Background
Task-oriented dialogue systems are primarily designed to search and interact with large databases which contain information pertaining to a certain dialogue domain: the main purpose of such systems is to assist the users in accomplishing a well-defined task such as flight booking BIBREF0, tourist information BIBREF1, restaurant search BIBREF2, or booking a taxi BIBREF3. These systems are typically constructed around rigid task-specific ontologies BIBREF1, BIBREF4 which enumerate the constraints the users can express using a collection of slots (e.g., price range for restaurant search) and their slot values (e.g., cheap, expensive for the aforementioned slots). Conversations are then modelled as a sequence of actions that constrain slots to particular values. This explicit semantic space is manually engineered by the system designer. It serves as the output of the natural language understanding component as well as the input to the language generation component both in traditional modular systems BIBREF5, BIBREF6 and in more recent end-to-end task-oriented dialogue systems BIBREF7, BIBREF8, BIBREF9, BIBREF3.
Working with such explicit semantics for task-oriented dialogue systems poses several critical challenges on top of the manual time-consuming domain ontology design. First, it is difficult to collect domain-specific data labelled with explicit semantic representations. As a consequence, despite recent data collection efforts to enable training of task-oriented systems across multiple domains BIBREF0, BIBREF3, annotated datasets are still few and far between, as well as limited in size and the number of domains covered. Second, the current approach constrains the types of dialogue the system can support, resulting in artificial conversations, and breakdowns when the user does not understand what the system can and cannot support. In other words, training a task-based dialogue system for voice-controlled search in a new domain always implies the complex, expensive, and time-consuming process of collecting and annotating sufficient amounts of in-domain dialogue data.
In this paper, we present a demo system based on an alternative approach to task-oriented dialogue. Relying on non-generative response retrieval we describe the PolyResponse conversational search engine and its application in the task of restaurant search and booking. The engine is trained on hundreds of millions of real conversations from a general domain (i.e., Reddit), using an implicit representation of semantics that directly optimizes the task at hand. It learns what responses are appropriate in different convers

We plan to experiment with more sophisticated multilingual models in future work.
Other Functionality ::: Voice-Controlled Menu Search.
An additional functionality enables the user to get parts of the restaurant menu relevant to the current user utterance as responses. This is achieved by performing an additional ranking step of available menu items and retrieving the ones that are semantically relevant to the user utterance using exactly the same methodology as with ranking other responses. An example of this functionality is shown in Figure FIGREF21.
Other Functionality ::: Resetting and Switching to Booking.
The restaurant search system needs to support the discrete actions of restarting the conversation (i.e., resetting the set $R$), and should enable transferring to the slot-based table booking flow. This is achieved using two binary intent classifiers, that are run at each step in the dialogue. These classifiers make use of the already-computed $h_c$ vector that represents the user's latest text. A single-layer neural net is learned on top of the 512-dimensional encoding, with a ReLU activation and 100 hidden nodes. To train the classifiers, sets of 20 relevant paraphrases (e.g., “Start again”) are provided as positive examples. Finally, when the system successfully switches to the booking scenario, it proceeds to the slot filling task: it aims to extract all the relevant booking information from the user (e.g., date, time, number of people to dine). The entire flow of the system illustrating both the search phase and the booking phase is provided as the supplemental video material.
Conclusion and Future Work
This paper has presented a general approach to search-based dialogue that does not rely on explicit semantic representations such as dialogue acts or slot-value ontologies, and allows for multi-modal responses. In future work, we will extend the current demo system to more tasks and languages, and work with more sophisticated encoders and ranking functions. Besides the initial dialogue flow from this work (§SECREF3), we will also work with more complex flows dealing, e.g., with user intent shifts.

In this paper, we present a demo system based on an alternative approach to task-oriented dialogue. Relying on non-generative response retrieval we describe the PolyResponse conversational search engine and its application in the task of restaurant search and booking. We describe a PolyReponse system that assists the users in finding a relevant restaurant according to their preference, and then additionally helps them to make a booking in the selected restaurant. Since retrieved system responses are presented visually to the user, the PolyResponse restaurant search engine is able to combine text responses with relevant visual information (e.g., photos from social media associated with the current restaurant and related to the user utterance), effectively yielding a multi-modal response. Finally, the PolyResponse restaurant search engine is multilingual: it is currently deployed in 8 languages enabling search over restaurants in 8 cities around the world. LLM summary / budget-adapted
Task-oriented dialogue systems traditionally assist users with specific tasks like flight booking, tourist information, restaurant search, or taxi booking by interacting with domain databases. These systems rely on manually engineered, rigid task-specific ontologies that define slots and values to model conversations as sequences of constraint actions. This explicit semantic representation serves as the interface between natural language understanding and generation components in both modular and end-to-end systems. However, this approach faces critical challenges: domain-specific data labeled with explicit semantics is difficult and expensive to collect, leading to limited annotated datasets; it constrains dialogue types, causing artificial conversations and breakdowns; and deploying a system in a new domain requires a complex, time-consuming process of data collection and annotation.

This paper presents a demo system, PolyResponse, which adopts an alternative, retrieval-based approach for task-oriented dialogue, specifically applied to restaurant search and booking. Instead of using explicit semantics, PolyResponse employs a non-generative response retrieval engine trained on hundreds of millions of real, general-domain conversations from Reddit. It learns implicit semantic representations by optimizing for appropriate responses in conversational contexts. The engine ranks a large pool of candidate responses based on their relevance to the current user utterance and dialogue history.

The underlying conversational search engine, detailed in prior work, computes two similarity scores: S(r,c) for a candidate text reply r given context c, and S(p,c) for a candidate photo p given context c. These are calculated as a scaled cosine similarity between a context vector (h_c) and vectors for the reply (h_r) or photo (h_p). The text representation model is a deep neural network trained on over 727 million Reddit context-reply pairs from January 2015 to December 2018. It uses a vocabulary of unigrams and bigrams, processes text with transformers and fully connected layers, and produces 512-dimensional encodings. Training maximizes similarity for true pairs and minimizes it for random negative pairs via SGD.

Photo representation uses a convolutional neural network (MobileNet) pretrained on ImageNet, producing a 1,792-dimensional vector that is passed through hidden layers to a final 512-dimensional representation h_p. The photo encoder is trained on the Yelp Open dataset (approximately 200K photos with captions) to maximize similarity between photo vectors and caption vectors encoded by the response encoder.

At inference, the system pre-computes response vectors for a pool of candidates. For restaurant search in a city, this pool includes: restaurant entities, photos (from Yelp and Google Places API), templated sentences from structured restaurant data (e.g., "Restaurant X accepts credit cards."), and sentences extracted from online reviews. Given a user context, it computes h_c and retrieves nearest neighbor text and photo responses efficiently using libraries like Faiss.

The system supports a multi-turn dialogue flow for narrowing down restaurant choices. The dialogue state is a set R of relevant restaurants, initialized to all restaurants in the city. For each user input, responses pertaining to restaurants in R are ranked. Probability scores are computed from the top N cosine similarities, aggregated per restaurant, and R is updated to the smallest set of restaurants whose aggregated scores exceed a threshold t. Responses are displayed accordingly; when only one restaurant remains, top responses and relevant photos are shown. The system uses simple predefined rules to generate spoken responses (e.g., "One review of e said r"). It does not require separate understanding, decision-making, or generation modules.

PolyResponse is multimodal, combining text responses with relevant visual information (e.g., social media photos). It supports both voice and text input/output, using off-the-shelf Google Cloud tools for speech-to-text and text-to-speech. The system is currently deployed in 8 languages for 8 cities: English (Edinburgh), German (Berlin), Spanish (Madrid), Mandarin (Taipei), Polish (Warsaw), Russian (Moscow), Korean (Seoul), and Serbian (Belgrade). Multilinguality is achieved via a translate-to-source approach: response pools are translated to English beforehand for encoding, and user utterances are translated to English on-the-fly.

Additional functionalities include: voice-controlled menu search, ranking menu items semantically relevant to user utterances using the same methodology; and intent classifiers to reset the dialogue state or switch to a separate slot-based table booking flow. These classifiers are single-layer neural nets on top of the h_c encoding, trained on paraphrases for actions like "Start again". The booking phase performs slot filling for details like date, time, and party size.

The retrieval-based design eliminates the need for engineered ontologies, general language generation, or dedicated policy modules. The large ranking model encapsulates knowledge about natural language and conversational flow from the Reddit training data. Future work aims to extend the system to more tasks and languages, employ more sophisticated encoders and ranking functions, and handle more complex dialogue flows such as user intent shifts.

Puka Rumi
Puka Rumi (Quechua puka red, rumi stone, "red stone", Hispanicized spelling Pucarumi) is a 5,000-metre-high (16,404 ft) mountain in the northern part of the Chunta mountain range in the Andes of Peru. It is situated in the Huancavelica Region, Huancavelica Province, Acobambilla District, and in the Junín Region, Huancayo Province, Chongos Alto District. Puka Rumi lies southeast of Ñawinqucha.

There are multiple mountains named Yana Urqu in the Andes. In Peru, one is about 4,800 meters high in the Cusco Region (Quispicanchi Province, Marcapata District), southwest of Wanakuni and west of Q'umirqucha lake. Another, about 5,000 meters high, is in the Willkanuta range in the same Cusco province and district, southwest of Q'illu Wallayuq and northeast of Yayamari. A third, approximately 4,800 meters high, is in the Willkanuta range in the same Cusco province and district, southeast of Jaqhichuwa.  Q'asa. A fifth, about 5,000 meters high, is in the north of the Wansu range in the Apurímac Region (Antabamba Province, Oropesa District), southwest of Willkarana and Kisu Qutu. A sixth, 4,890 meters high, is in the Huancavelica Region (Huancavelica Province, Huacocolpa District), southeast of Chapi Urqu and northeast of Inqhana. A seventh, about 5,000 meters high, is in the Chunta range in the Huancavelica Region (Huancavelica Province, Huacocolpa District), northwest of Inqhana and northeast of Wayra Q'asa. In Bolivia, Yana Urqu is a 3,572-meter-high mountain in the Cochabamba Department (Mizque Province, Mizque Municipality). The Yana Urqu Mayu river originates northwest of it and flows to the Mizque River.
